Mr. Speaker, I was a member of the Committee on Indian Affairs and Northern Development which drafted and presented to the House a report on Arctic sovereignty which, as has been mentioned several times, had the unanimous endorsation of all the members of that committee. Therefore, I believe it should be apparent that I am as concerned as any member of the House that we should make a clear declaration of Canadian sovereignty over the waters which lie between the islands of the Arctic archipelago.
I took an active part in the debate on the amendments to the Canada Shipping Act. Had those amendments passed, they would have placed the liability for the cost of incidents such as occurred off the coast of Nova Scotia- I refer to the break-up of the Arrow oil tanker -on the owners of the vessel or cargo. Therefore, I do not quarrel at all with the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin) with regard to the need for exercising complete Canadian control over the passage of oil tankers through Arctic waters.
I have often enjoyed the reasoned and cogent arguments presented in this House by the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka (Mr. Aiken) and the hon. member for Peace

February 13. 1970
Oil and Gas Act
River, but their arguments today in support of the amendment which they placed before the House are a little beyond my comprehension. I am not too good at some of the long words, but I think the proper word to use in respect of the amendment is that they have completely obfuscated the matter of Arctic sovereignty. Therefore, at the outset I should like to make clear that I have no intention of supporting the motion for a six months' hoist, which we ordinarily understand to be one to kill a proposal. I believe my view is shared by my colleagues in the New Democratic Party.
The hon. member for Peace River referred to clause 3 of the bill and pointed out that it contains what was in the act passed last year, which is now chapter 48 of the statutes. Clause 3 refers to the Yukon territory and Northwest Territories. That part of the bill was passed, and I submit with deference to the learned gentleman from Peace River that what was the Yukon territory and the Northwest Territories last year is still the Yukon territory and the Northwest Territories. Therefore, nothing in this bill in any way detracts from the area of Canada encompassed by the Yukon territory and the Northwest Territories.
If I understand this proposal correctly, we are talking about the sea bed; we are not talking about the geographical boundaries of Canada. If the waters within the Arctic archipelago rightfully are internal waters of Canada, and therefore part of the Northwest Territories, this fact is not in any way lessened or detracted from by the proposals in this bill.
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)
What is important is that we are saying we intend to exercise sovereignty over the continental shelf which is rightly ours as a result of the Geneva convention which gave the sea bed to the adjacent coastal states. Therefore, we must consider this whole proposition, realizing that we are talking, not only about the Arctic Ocean and the sea bed under it but about the Pacific Ocean and the Atlantic Ocean.
Far from weakening the position with regard to our sovereignty in the Arctic, I suggest this bill may strengthen it. I do not have the chart to which the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka (Mr. Aiken) referred. However, I suggest that an examination of that chart may very well show that certain areas north of the Canadian mainland which this bill will cover in so far as the exploita-

tion of oil, gas and other resources of the sea bed are concerned, would not be included in an exercise of sovereignty which would include as internal waters those lying between the islands of the Arctic archipelago and the mainland.
I will not go into the question of the sector theory, but I just throw the suggestion that at least so far as the argument about jurisdiction over territorial sea or inland waters is concerned, this bill does not weaken our position. Therefore, I think the argument for its delay on the grounds advanced by the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka and the hon. member for Peace River falls to the ground. I hope they appreciate that I am not in any way discounting their concern that our government take a firm position on the question of our exercise of sovereignty. We in this party are with them on that point.
If one were to consider the question of whether we should go slow on the provisions of this bill, one might come to the conclusion that perhaps of greater concern is the question raised by my colleagues, the hon. member for Battleford-Kindersley (Mr. Thomson) and the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Harding), namely, the question of the potential danger to Canada and to future generations of Canadians of any sort of oil exploitation in underwater areas.
The examples they mentioned of the California coast and the incident which is fresh in our minds-which is not directly related to the bill-of the destruction of the oil tanker and the resulting serious harm to the ecology of the east coast, should put this matter very much to the fore when we consider a proposal for the exploration of oil and gas in underwater areas within the boundaries of the continental shelf.
With this point in mind I have examined the act that was passed last session, with particular reference to the authority which, as has already been pointed out by my colleagues and others taking part in the debate, has not been exercised-in this case the authority of the Governor in Council to make regulations. The act as it now stands does give some authority in section 12 (m), (p) and (q). I think it is important before this bill passes through the committee stage, at least for the government to make clear the substance of the regulation which it intends to enforce in respect of these paragraphs of the section. In order to underline the point I am
February 13, 1970

trying to make, I should like to read them. The paragraphs read as follows:
(m) prescribing the conditions under which drilling operations may be carried out in water-covered areas and any special measures to be taken for such operations; ...
(p)	prescribing minimum acceptable standards for the construction, alteration or use of any works, fittings, machinery, plant and appliances used for the development, production, transmission, distribution, measurement, storage or handling of any oil or gas;
(q)	prescribing the measures necessary to prevent pollution of air, land or water as a result of the exploration and drilling for or the production, storage, transportation, distribution, measurement, processing or handling of any oil, or gas or any substance obtained from or associated with oil or gas;
We are considering an amending bill which in effect says that we will take steps to control the exploration, development and utilization of oil, gas and other resources which may exist under the sea bed adjacent to our coast on any of the three oceans. Therefore, members of the House, members of the committee and the Canadian people should know in detail how the government intends to exercise the authority conferred upon it under those paragraphs of section 12 of the Oil and Gas Production and Conservation Act which was passed by the House last year.
It seems to me logical that if there is to be a pause at any point in our proceedings on this bill, it should be at the committee stage until the committee is thoroughly satisfied that the steps the government is taking under the authority granted it in those paragraphs will be exercised in a manner consistent with the preservation of other aspects of our environment. The committee should also ensure that the exploitation of oil and gas reserves is carried out in a way that will not cause damage which outweighs its economic advantage.
In this connection I should like to quote briefly from a statement made recently by a person who some would say is quite knowledgeable in this area:
Protection, however, is a difficult subject. In recent years we have been mesmerised by technology. We have been mesmerised by advances on the scientific front-advances which have been concerned mainly with physics and inorganic chemistry, with electronics and nuclear power.
[DOT] (3:50 p.m.)
But the unique thing about our planet, about our earth, about our water, is that it harbours living things. Ours is a living planet in a lifeless universe. And yet our modern technology has been concerned, much more, with lifeless things. It has been concerned about lifeless space, about instant communications and about the generation of power.

Our study of life itself, by comparison, is in its infancy. Biology has been, to some extent, neglected. Ecology, even though it deals with the inter-relationship of living things, is a new word. Perhaps these inter-relationships are too complex for us to understand. But we must know more about these life-giving processes, these living cycles, these vital inter-relationships. We must know about them for our own good and for the good of life itself.
What worries people most are the immense powers which inanimate science-lifeless science-
I suppose one could say the immense powers proposed for the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Greene).
-has given us to destroy life on this planet. If these new powers are used thoughtlessly our biological balance will be upset.
I would like to have heard that statement made in this House by its author, because it is a statement made by the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Davis). I have hardly ever quoted in this House a statement made by a member of the government with more approbation than I do those remarks of the Minister of Fisheries. The sad thing is that it was not a statement of government policy, because it was prefaced with the words:
I would like to make one thing quite clear at the outset. I am speaking as a Member of Parliament.
In other words, he emphasized that he was not expressing government policy. I suggest it is a rather sad thing when the Minister of Fisheries has to go off into a corner to some little Liberal workshop in Capilano to make a statement of that kind, rather than getting up in this House, in a debate such as this, and making it as a statement of policy of the government concerning the exploitation of the inanimate resources of our country.
The considerations expressed by the hon. member for Capilano are the important things which should be in the minds of members of the committee when this bill is being discussed in detail. In committee we should have answers to the kind of questions which he raised in that statement, before the committee reports the bill back to the House. As we are all becoming increasingly aware, these are not matters to be dealt with lightly.
My colleague from Kootenay West made brief reference to a statement about the delicate balance of the ecology of the Arctic. The northern affairs committee has had quite a number of representations made to it on this subject and has discussed the matter. Some of its concern is indicated in its report to this House. That report has been only partially debated, and we have no indication that the House will ever be allowed to come to a decision on it.

The contents of this bill are of immediate concern to a member who comes from the province of British Columbia, because of the oil exploration that was carried out on the sea bed of the coast of B.C. a year or so ago. This exploration was in the outer waters lying offshore from the west coast of my constituency, and more recently in the inside waters of Georgia Strait. This bill, if passed, will become operative in respect of all or part of those areas. I say all or part, Mr. Speaker, because the question of the jurisdiction over certain areas is still up in the air. According to statements made in this House on earlier occasions, the Strait of Georgia is one of those areas. Whether it will come within the ambit of this bill is open to question. Of course if the proposal contained in the remarks of the Minister of Fisheries about an underwater park is implemented, we may not have to worry about whether a federal or provincial minister is involved in the granting of oil permits for drilling in the Strait of Georgia. The suggestion made to the Minister of Northern Affairs (Mr. Chretien) by the Minister of Fisheries, if it has not already been well noted should be well noted by the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources.
There is another point I would like to make on this issue. It has been touched upon during question periods, when we sought to obtain clarification of the status of waters such as the Strait of Georgia so far as oil exploration and the issuing of oil leases are concerned. Unless the situation has changed quite recently, the minister told us that an offer was made to British Columbia to put Georgia Strait under provincial jurisdiction, but that there had been no indication from the government of that province as to whether it was prepared to take ac ion on the offer. I suggest that, whether or not we are to have an underwater park in Georgia Strait, enough time has elapsed since that offer was made to the government of British Columbia that the federal government should now announce that the offer is withdrawn.
I say that, Mr. Speaker, at least in part because it is obvious that the Premier of British Columbia, who sometimes seems to imagine he is a sort of tin-pot emperor, is not prepared to sit down and discuss any question intelligently with the government of Canada. At least, if he does it is a very exceptional situation. I want to make it clear in this House-

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to make a few comments on the bill introduced by the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Leblanc) and in so doing to state my general support for what it is broadly intended to cover. However, I must make two reservations that apply to the bill. In the final analysis, I think it should go to the Standing Committee on Transport and


Communications, there to be more closely scrutinized with the help of expert witnesses who might be called.
My first qualification is this: In these days transportation is not a single factor but a total mix. Transportation involves all forms of transport which are important to our economy. More important, not only must transportation efficiently move objects being transported, but we must ask ourselves whether any particular mode of transport gives to the user the best possible service. We all know that in Canada today our national railways are deeply involved in road transportation and no one really suggests, nor does this bill suggest, that this is improper. Quite the contrary is true. There are many indications that where rail service has been cut back or abandoned in recent years in certain parts of the country, the people living in the areas affected have suffered very serious privation.
My other qualification relates to the widespread use of varying modes of transportation by railway companies, and in particular I refer to air transport. The explanatory note to the bill is as follows:
The purpose of this hill is to provide that no railway company receiving moneys from the government of Canada or from any agency thereof may acquire interest or control in motor vehicle transport undertaking; the said undertakings receiving no subvention or subsidies from the state and being free enterprises, it is only fair that the said railway companies be not subsidized in part for acquiring such free enterprises.
My qualifications relate in part to the utilization of other forms of transport in connection with air freight. What do these words mean, "The purpose of this bill is to provide that no railway company receiving moneys from the Government of Canada"? There are many ways in which companies owning a broad range of transportation facilities can receive money directly or indirectly from the government. As part of my qualified support of the bill I ask that it be sent to the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications for further study in connection with this question.
My next comment relates to a fear which exists in many parts of Atlantic Canada. Under our present law there is nothing to prevent the government of Canada pouring a tremendous amount of money into Sept lies and developing a modern container port there. Indeed, this House has before it recommendations that a container-port ought to be developed. As a member of the Standing
February 13, 1970	COMMONS DEBATES	3603
Committee on Transport and Communications, I hope the government will move swiftly on that recommendation.
If the bill is intended to provide protection against railway companies moving into the Sept lies area and operating trucks to the west of the Saguenay River system, I am against it. On the other hand, if it is trying to create a monopoly or near-monopoly in the area, my support for the bill becomes virtually unqualified. As I have said, it is the total transportation package that hon. members must be concerned about. We must make sure that all Canadians obtain the most efficient transportation service available.
Further, I should not like to see Canadian National Railways or, for that matter, any railway company tie up all modes of transport to Sept lies-which as hon. members may know is not served by rail along the shore of the river-to the extent that a monopoly might be created which could disrupt efforts being made in the port of Halifax to develop an efficient container service. We cannot support too many container ports. This aspect of the matter worries me in view of our National Transportation Act. There is nothing in the act to prevent that happening. I am not saying that a single agency could do it, but that situation might develop.
On the other hand, I should hate to see this virtual monopoly being given to any railway company without there being recourse for redress by this House. The absence of such recourse would have a disastrous effect on the work being done at public expense in Halifax. It seems to me there is not room for two or three container ports. Speaking for myself, if the bill we are considering provides some protection against a so-called monopoly, that could be detrimental. I urge hon. members to consider having these and related questions referred to the committee, which should also look at the wide powers the National Transportation Act has with relation to modes of transport serving areas which constitute a captive market.
On these two grounds, and with these two minor qualifications, I support the bill. The first qualification is that we must accept transportation as a total package and not as something that can be separated into different modes. The other one is the detrimental effect it could have on other areas of Canada and the absence of control of the National Transportation Act if a single agency determined to move in this way. I congratulate the mover of the bill and urge that it be referred to the standing committee for further consideration.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to take part briefly in the debate on Bill C-25. I was particularly pleased to hear the hon. member who preceded me speak about the monopolistic attitude of the railway companies and other companies in Canada. As a member of the transport committee, I believe that our main purpose is to ensure that all Canadians are provided with the most effective and efficient transportation system. I am sure this is exactly what the hon. member for Dartmouth-Halifax East (Mr. Forrestall) meant. He is concerned about a monopoly being instituted in this country which will take over all forms of transportation.
I express some doubt about this bill. We must all realize it is too late and too little, in a general context, to be an effective measure at this time. All of us in the standing committee who visited the maritimes not long ago realized that truck transportation is included under the Maritime Freight Rates Act. I believe if we were to propose a bill at this time dealing with railways only, we would soon have to propose an amendment to the National Transportation Act to deal with trucking systems.
I am sure all those who feel we should keep this country united from east to west realize we must have an efficient trucking system. We are not really looking at the over-all monopoly end of it when we talk about allowing the railways into the trucking industry. The main concern of this House should be that we provide an efficient transportation system.
If the transportation users of this country are to receive the type of consideration they should, naturally we have to look at the entire transportation system. I am not sure of the words of the member who introduced Bill C-25 when he stated that the United States prohibited any form of competition in this field. In the explanatory note it is said that the purpose of the bill is to provide that no railways company receiving moneys from the government of Canada or any agency thereof may acquire interest or control in motor vehicles. I have not gone into the general field to the same extent as the hon. member, but I wonder whether some of the railway companies in the United States also have an interest in trucking concerns. I am not prepared to express an opinion on that matter.
If we are really concerned about railway companies receiving moneys from the federal
February 13, 1970

National Transportation Act government and entering into competition with trucking companies, we must say the same about trucking companies competing in any other field. If we are worried about a monopoly in one field, we must be worried about a monopoly in all fields. It should be very clear that if this bill is referred to the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications, these questions should be dealt with. More explanation must be given to the House before I will support the bill.

subsubtopic: PROVISION THAT RAILWAY COMPANIES RECEIVING GOVERNMENT SUBSIDY SHALL NOT ACQUIRE INTEREST IN MOTOR VEHICLE TRANSPORT UNDERTAKINGS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I take pleasure in participating in this debate on Bill C-25. As indicated in the explanatory note, the purpose of this bill is to provide that railway companies which receive subventions or subsidies from the government do not purchase or control trucking concerns. I wish to state at the outset that I do not think taxpayers' money should be used to compete with free enterprise. In other words, I do not agree with subsidies being given under the National Transportation Act or the Maritime Freight Rates Act to help railway companies compete with the trucking industry.
The purpose of this bill is not only to ensure that the railway companies do not purchase trucking companies; it is specified that the railway companies which receive subventions or subsidies should not acquire control of trucking companies. It should be pointed out that there is a slight difference here. These subsidies should not give to the railway companies an unfavourable advantage in competing with independent truckers.
I was a member of the committee which visited the Atlantic provinces and the north shore of Quebec last year. I was present at the transport committee meeting at Levis when the president of the Canadian Association of Truckers presented his case. My impression of Mr. Charbonneau's testimony was not that he was so much concerned about any particular subsidy being given to the railway companies, but that this indirectly gave the railway companies an advantage over the independent truckers. 1 do not agree with him. The record must clearly indicate that even though the CNR receives subventions or subsidies from the government of Canada, this does not mean that in the operation of truck freight or express delivery it is competing with the trucking industry.
We must bear in mind that the railway companies maintain their own track systems. In addition to operating expenses they have large capital expenses which independent companies do not have. The Canadian truck-

ing industry does not have to pay for the roads it uses. It does not have to maintain the roads. I appreciate that they pay sales tax and fuel tax, but they do not have the responsibilities that the railways have.
I was amused when the president of the Association of Truckers said that the trucking industry was at a disadvantage because the railway companies were operating trucking companies. His testimony differed from that of Mr. Palmer, the president of the Atlantic Association of Truckers who appeared before the committee in Fredericton last year. Mr. Palmer said the trucking industry in the Atlantic provinces was not concerned that the CNR or CPR may purchase trucking companies in the Atlantic provinces. He clearly stated that the trucking industry in the mari-times could meet that competition so long as the railways did not manipulate their invoices and waybills in a way that would take advantage of the Maritime Freight Rates Act when they were making deliveries by truck.
[DOT] (4:30 p.m.)
Mr. Palmer made the allegation that the CNR was receiving a subsidy from the government of Canada under the Maritime Freight Rates Act to transport goods, say from Montreal to Moncton. Then supposing material was to be shipped to Sussex, 40 miles from Moncton, and could not be transported by rail for one reason or another, the CNR would collect a subsidy on the part of the route from Moncton to Sussex. That part of the route would still be covered by the MFRA.
When Mr. McDougall, the vice-president of the CN Atlantic area, was before the committee, he said this only happened when the railway company had operated a station at the point earlier and had then closed it down. I am repeating what Mr. McDougall said: He told the committee that in no instance did the CN use the subsidy to compete directly with the trucking industry.
I am drawing attention to the conflict between the view of the president of the Canadian association and that of the president of the Atlantic association. The president of the Atlantic association said clearly that he was not concerned about the CNR and CPR buying trucking concerns in the Atlantic provinces, because he felt his people could compete with them.
I return to the principle of whether the railway companies should or should not enter the trucking business. I should like to see this
February 13, 1970

issue discussed and decided by Parliament. In other words, Parliament should decide whether the railway companies should be permitted to buy-out trucking operators. I am not sure whether it would be advantageous to prevent their doing so. It seems to me that the trucking industry is trying to preserve its interests. If it could get rid of its biggest competitors, CN and CPR, it would be better off. I do not see anything wrong with Canadian Pacific and Canadian National going into the trucking business so long as they do not use the subsidies they receive from the government to this end. It leads to better competition; it leads to more efficient service; it keeps the trucking industry on the ball.

Mr. Speaker, I agree with the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Leblanc) that the trucking industry has made a significant contribution to the economic expansion of our country.
During the hearings held in Levis by the Transport and Communications Committee, it was pointed out that Northern Quebec, for example, had been developed exclusively through the trucking industry, and the same is true of the paper industry in the Chibouga-mau area.
There is no question of belittling the part played by the trucking industry, but it is unfair to say merely that the Canadian National, the Canadian Pacific or some other railway company are using government subsidies to purchase trucks or trucking companies.
In my opinion, we should make sure that the grants will not directly be used in an unfair competition with the trucking industry.
Before concluding my comments, I would like to say a few words about the M.F.R.A. grants, a question which was raised by Mr. Palmer before the members of the committee in Fredericton. Indeed, I would have liked the Canadian Transport Commission to decide whether really the C.N.R. or the C.P.R. in the Atlantic provinces were entitled, thanks to the M.F.R.A. grants, to pay the transportation costs of products by truck. This issue seemed to me very confusing. In other words, the Canadian National somewhat deviated from the principle under which the M.F.R.A. applied only to railway transportation. Of course, before the passing last summer of the legislation on the assistance to trucking in the Atlantic provinces, I would have liked the Canadian Transport Commission to render a decision which would have indicated whether the C.N.R. had acted in a legal way.
National Transportation Act [English]

subtopic: NATIONAL TRANSPORTATION ACT
subsubtopic: PROVISION THAT RAILWAY COMPANIES RECEIVING GOVERNMENT SUBSIDY SHALL NOT ACQUIRE INTEREST IN MOTOR VEHICLE TRANSPORT UNDERTAKINGS
speechtext:
This is quite a controversial bill, Mr. Speaker, and I should like to compliment the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Leblanc) for bringing it in. Although it is not a government measure, it is one to which we should give a good deal of study. Railways subsidized by the treasury are entering the trucking industry to an increasing extent. In many cases these railway companies have behaved very unjustly toward a lot of settlements. I say this because they did not complete the branch lines which they had been given charters to build. This resulted in many injustices to communities in my constituency.
Now the railways are trying to put private trucking companies out of business. Since they are subsidized in the first place, they can very easily do this. They can haul in trucks Piggy-back most of the way, and then put private enterprise out of business. It is likely that small truckers pioneered this business in the first place, the railways companies not having thought it worth while to complete the branch lines they had been au horized to build. This is a situation which deserves close study by all hon. members. We have all seen what the railways can do by moving trucks piggy-back over the long haul and then delivering within a district by road.
It is possible that some of these communities would never have received the benefits of a trucking service had not private businessmen been enterprising enough to provide it. Now, apparently, the railway companies intend to put the private firms out of business. I believe they are again taking advantage of the rural communities in their master station plan. They are doing a disservice to many of these places by removing the station agent and using through-trains. Now the attempt is being made to put the small trucker out of business.
[DOT] (4:40 p.m.)
I think this matter warrants very careful consideration before we allow any company which has been subsidized to this extent to compete against private enterprise and push other companies around, as they very easily could. Many companies were prevented from building lines because the national railways had the charter, even though they never fulfilled their part of the bargain. Many truck lines would not have been required had these rail lines been completed. I think the House should take a good look at the bill before giving it passage.
February 13, 1970

National Transportation Act

subtopic: NATIONAL TRANSPORTATION ACT
subsubtopic: PROVISION THAT RAILWAY COMPANIES RECEIVING GOVERNMENT SUBSIDY SHALL NOT ACQUIRE INTEREST IN MOTOR VEHICLE TRANSPORT UNDERTAKINGS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, with some regularity in the past we have condemned and criticized our railroads for their lack of aggressiveness and their complacency. It is my understanding that an article which appeared recently in the "Harvard Business Review"-it has apparently been their most requested reprint-used the railroads as the classic example of what they called "marketing myopia". It was said to be the industry that has shown outstanding lack of imagination and lack of initiative.
At the turn of the century the railroads were dominant and all-powerful. It is my understanding that somewhere along the line Sir Edward Beattie remarked that he would far rather be president of the CPR than prime minister of Canada. Yet half a century later one finds throughout North America the majority of the railroads in receivership, in bankruptcy, or surviving on subsidies paid them by governments. Certainly they suffered during this period from marketing myopia and allowed the trucking industry, the airlines, the bus companies and pipelines to take over a substantial part of their market. They conceived of themselves as being in the railroad business,, not in the business of transporting people and moving goods, or in the business of serving or developing markets.
As I said, Mr. Speaker, they suffered from marketing myopia and belatedly have been shaking off their lethargy; and now as we move into the last half of the 20th century it is my opinion that this bill proposes to push them back into the railroad industry and to once more limit their vision.
Bill C-25 proposes that if a railway receives subsidies or moneys from the government, it may not acquire, directly or indirectly, any interest or control in a trucking firm. If there was a way in which the railways could misuse subsidies paid to them for the purpose of buying truck lines, one could readily support the principle of this bill. The intention of the National Transportation Act is to enable all modes of transport to compete on fair conditions. The government does not propose to make taxpayer's money available to the railways for the purpose of buying up independently-owned trucking firms.
There are three points to be made about Bill C-25. First is the nature of the subsidies that the railways receive; the fact that each subsidy is paid to the railways for a specific purpose that does not include the purchase of truck lines and that leaves nothing extra for the railways to use on that account. The second point is that there is a provision in the
[Mr. Cadieu (Meadow-Lake) .1

Railway Act that bars any railway under federal jurisdiction from mixing up its railway and trucking accounts in a way that would enable the trucking operation to obtain indirectly any subsidy from the government. The third point is that there exists in the National Transportation Act a specific provision, the object of which is to prevent acquisition in the transportation field which will unduly restrict competition or otherwise adversely affect the public interest.
Although the railways receive, as yet, no subsidies for passenger services, they are entitled to such subsidies if the Canadian Transport Commission determines that a service they operate at a loss must be continued in the public interest. The railways will have no money from this source to play around with in regard to truck line purchases. The National Transportation Act does not permit any extra in compensating the railways for passenger losses. The appropriate section does not permit compensation for the full loss which the railroads incurred. I understand they get approximately 80 per cent of the loss, which has to be certified by the commission.
The only large-scale subsidy that the Canadian railways receive is what is left of the subsidy that had its origin in the Freight Rates Reduction Act of 1959. That act reduced railway non-competitive class and commodity rates and provided $20 million to the railways in compensation for their revenue loss. By 1967 the $20 million in annual rail subsidies had risen to $110 million. There had been two more wage settlements. Rail rates remained frozen. The policy of governments of that day, both Conservative and Liberal, was to restrain further across-the-board freight rate increases pending the introduction of new national transportation legislation and they continued to compensate the railways for the revenue losses incurred as the result of the freight rate freeze.
Railway rates were frozen in 1959, and for a period of seven years did not move upward. Operating costs were not frozen; on the contrary, they were increasing substantially. The losses sustained by the railways in not being able to raise their rates were compensated from the federal treasury. When there is on the one hand a frozen price structure, and on the other hand a situation of substantially increasing costs, it is obvious that nowhere can a subsidy be applied except in the situation for which the subsidy is created, namely, the defraying of losses sustained. There is no
February 13. 1970	COMMONS
evidence to sustain a contention that subsidies given to the railroads have played a significant, or any, part in their acquisition of truck lines.
I think another significant point, and one of which we should be aware, is that the large-scale subsidy to which I have just referred and which amounted to roughly $120 million in 1967 has since been going down each year at the rate of $14 million. At the end of the fiscal year 1974 it will have disappeared. The railways received $96 million in 1968, $82 million in 1969, and will get $68 million in 1970, and so on, on a reducing scale, with a final payment of $12 million in 1974.
Another concern one must have about this question, one that quite possibly the author of the bill had in mind when he framed it, is that even if a railway has no opportunity to finance the purchase of a truck line either wholly or in part from subsidy moneys paid to it, does the rail carrier not have the opportunity, once the purchase is made, to inject into its truck line financial sustenance drawn from government subsidies or other moneys?
The answer is that the law requires the railway companies to maintain separate accounting of the assets and earnings of their rail and non-rail enterprises. The law also requires that the railways maintain separate accounting of the operation of their various modes of transport. If, for example, a railway company operates a railway, subsidiary truck lines, an airline and steamships, the accounts for each mode shall be separately maintained. The object of this requirement of the law is to prevent cross-subsidization of rail and rail-controlled modes of transport.
These provisions impose responsibility for enforcement upon the Canadian Transport Commission. To ensure that the conditions set out are met, the commission is required by section 387 to review and revise the uniform classification of accounts at intervals no longer than every two years.
[DOT] (4:50 p.m.)
The third point emphasized was the statutory protection of the public that already exists in the National Transportation Act. In the context of section 20 of that act, one of the stituations covered is the purchase of a truck line by a railway and the possibility of restriction of competition or the creation of a monopolistic situation which might work against the public interest. The act provides that in the case of an objection, the Canadian Transport Commission, following an investi-
DEBATES	3607
National Transportation Act gation which it must conduct, may disallow the proposed acquisition of that truck line by a railway if it is the commission's opinion that the acquisition would unduly restrict competition or otherwise be prejudicial to the public interest.
Subsidies paid to Canadian railways are of a nature that leaves nothing for the purchase of truck lines. In addition, the National Transportation Act contains safeguards for the public interest in respect of acquisition by a railway of a competing truck line. I believe it is the hope of all Canadians that an integrated road-rail system can reduce the distribution cost in our country, and that by combining the advantages of low-cost rail transportation with the flexible advantages of highway delivery our transportation systems can assist in opening up high-cost, low-volume markets. Canada is too vast and sparsely populated to be deprived of the very obvious advantages of an integrated road-rail system. It seems to me that is the intent of this bill and I therefore find myself in opposition to the principles it embraces.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as this is a private member's bill I shall be brief in my remarks because I think it should probably come to a vote. It is obviously not the intention of the government to protect private enterprise, because if it were this would be a government measure. I see a necessity in this socialistic state which we are rapidly approaching for some protection for private enterprise. This is the reason I speak in favour of the bill. I see the necessity, however, for the railways to be a paying proposition. But I suggest that if the railways streamlined their operations properly they would not find it necessary to engage in the private enterprise trucking industry.
I join my colleague the hon. member for Meadow Lake (Mr. Cadieu) in reminding the railways that their policy over the past 40 years has been strictly selfish. They do not try to give proper service according to the charter under which they were set in operation. The railways claim they have continually lost money in operating passenger service. One speaker mentioned they have had no compensation for this loss. They have not had compensation in cash grants for the loss, but one need only look at the vast holdings, especially of the CPR, to see that they have been paid in the form of oil and mineral rights alone, not to mention the real estate they own in every major city of Canada. I venture to
3608	COMMONS
National Transportation Act suggest that if they sold their rights-of-way at present real estate prices in any major city in Canada, they would be compensated for all the losses they have ever suffered in providing the transportation services they have provided.
When the railways have lost money they have always been able to come to the federal government, unlike ordinary free enterprise, and have the government come to then-rescue. During one particular depression year the CPR received no less than $60 million in t e form of an outright gift. Indeed, at one time it would have been better to have been head of the CPR than prime minister of Canada. With socialism rushing upon us, I am afraid a bill of this type is needed to protect the private citizen of Canada. I hope members of this House will stand, be counted and say that this bill should at least be passed in principle.

speakeroldname: Mr. James A. McGrath (St. John's East):
subtopic: MR. McGRATH-PHASING OUT OF ARGENTIA NAVAL BASE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege under Standing Order 17. At 4.30 p.m. this afternoon, Newfoundland time, an announcement was made in Newfoundland that the Argentia naval base would be phased out and that approximately 600 Canadian citizens employed on this United States installation would be laid off on 30 days' notice.
February 13, 1970

My question of privilege is based upon the fact that we have raised this question in the House on a number of occasions. I rise in my place today on behalf of my colleague the hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Carter) who is not aware that this has taken place because he is now on his way to Newfoundland. My colleague the hon. member for St. John's West, myself and other hon. members have raised this question in the House on a number of occasions.
[DOT] (5:00 p.m.)
Clearly, there is a responsibility on the part of the government of Canada. We find it reprehensible and an act of gross irresponsibility that this announcement should have been made in the way it was by the commander of the base. We feel that if there was to be an announcement of this nature, inevitable though it may have been, it should have been made in the House of Commons. It was only this morning, before the House convened for the day's sitting, that I directed a private inquiry to the government to ask what was the status of the U.S. naval base at Argentia at the present time. I was told that they did not know, and that telegrams were being exchanged back and forth.
Privilege
I find it difficult, if not impossible, to imagine that this announcement would have been made without the advice or consent of either the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Cadieux) or the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Sharp). This is a crippling, crushing blow to the already crippled economy of Newfoundland which is currently suffering the consequences of an unemployment rate in excess of 20 per cent.
I rise today on this question of privilege to serve notice that we should expect a statement from the government, when the House meets on Monday on exactly how the government can reconcile this announcement, made in the manner in which it was, with its statements in the House and with the current activities of the Department of Regional Economic Expansion. Clearly, the responsibility is placed squarely on the shoulders of this government to act very quickly.
